title: How the Rules of War Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the rules of war, tracing their origins from per-battle agreements to the 1859 Solferino battlefield that inspired the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention in 1864. They cover the Hague Conventions (including pre-war steps and declarations of war), rules on combat and weaponry, protections for the wounded, sick and dead, prisoners of war, civilians under occupation, cultural property, and how violations are punished through international tribunals and the International Criminal Court. They use Red Dawn, Inglorious Basterds, Shutter Island and Abu Ghraib as examples. The episode ends with a listener mail from Clovis about addiction treatment and drug-use statistics.

segments.title: Opening banter and Dachau story
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter and bring up the 1945 Dachau shooting of SS guards by American liberators, a story connected to the film Shutter Island, and note that the rules of war were violated.

segments.title: Origins of the rules of war
segments.summary: Before the nineteenth century, rules of war were set per battle and dropped after each conflict. In 1859 Henry Dunant treated wounded soldiers after the Battle of Solferino, which led to the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention in 1864.

segments.title: Geneva Conventions and their expansion
segments.summary: The Geneva Conventions grew over time to cover sick and shipwrecked sailors, prisoners of war, and civilians, with the fourth convention ratified in 1954. After World War Two, most countries joined, and about 190 have ratified them.

segments.title: Hague Conventions and pre-war steps
segments.summary: The Hague Conventions, from the International Peace Conferences in the Netherlands, cover combat, weaponry, property and neutral duties. They require steps to prevent war such as cooling-off periods, mediation and formal declarations of war, and the hosts link this to the democratic peace theory.

segments.title: Rules on combat, weapons and the wounded
segments.summary: Combatants may not attack surrendering or injured people, use human shields, attack hospitals, desecrate flags, use poison or chemical and biological weapons, or use dogs and similar weapons. Wounded and sick must be helped, and the dead must receive proper burial with graves registration and return of property.

segments.title: Prisoners of war
segments.summary: POWs are prisoners of the detaining country, escape is illegal unless they reach their own side, and officers receive better treatment. POW status applies to militia, war correspondents and others, and POWs must be treated humanely, given basic rights and allowed mail. Abu Ghraib is cited as an illegal case because detainees were not granted POW status.

segments.title: Civilians under occupation and Red Dawn
segments.summary: Using the film Red Dawn as an example, the hosts describe protections for civilians in occupied territory: limited correspondence, no forced transfer, no settling of the occupier's civilians, paid forced labor that cannot be used against their own country, and a ban on tattooing civilians.

segments.title: Cultural property, enforcement and tribunals
segments.summary: Museums, libraries, art, and archaeological sites are protected, and states must identify them. The conventions leave punishment to the injured country. Nuremberg, the Yugoslavia and Rwanda tribunals, and the International Criminal Court in The Hague are described, along with militia rules and the reciprocity logic behind compliance.

segments.title: Listener mail: Clovis on addiction
segments.summary: Listener Clovis writes that the earlier addiction episode overstated the success of Alcoholics Anonymous and that drug use rates are a poor measure of drug policy success. He argues treatment should be judged by reductions in death, disease, crime and suffering.
